newsitem.title: FRANCE: World leaders praise Hebron as milestone to peace.
newsitem.headline: World leaders praise Hebron as milestone to peace.

text.p: World leaders on Wednesday heaped praise on Palestinian and Israeli leaders for their agreement to extend Arab rule to the West Bank town of Hebron and said it was a milestone on the uphill road to Middle East peace.
A discordant note came from 81-year-old hardliner and former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, who predicted an early death for a deal he denounced as a defeat for the Jewish state.

On the border between Israel and the Gaza Strip on Tuesday night, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat sealed the accord on Hebron and agreed the timing for more Israeli withdrawals from occupied Arab land.
U.S. President Bill Clinton hailed the Hebron pact as a key step toward "a lasting, secure Middle East peace", adding that it was not a time to relax but to press on with cooperation.
Clinton praised both Netanyahu and Arafat, but U.S. officials said it was the President's personal involvement that helped clinch the deal after weeks of difficult bargaining.
"We'll do everything we can to build a just and durable peace, a peace that will mean a better life for Israelis, Palestinians, for all people of the Middle East," Clinton said.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl sent a telegram to Arafat and Netanyahu addressing them both as "dear friend" and welcoming the Hebron agreement.
"I see this as an important step for the continuation of the peace process," Kohl said.

Norway, mediator of the 1993 Israeli-Palestinian peace accords, expressed its happiness over the development, but Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal said he hoped the peace process would once again gain momentum after long delays.

The European Union congratulated both Israel and the Palestinians, saying it was an important step towards just and stable peace. "It can provide new momentum that is necessary to reinvigorate the peace process," said Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, who currently holds the EU presidency.
China, praising the deal, stressed the principle of exchanging peace for occupied Arab land.

"We hope sincerely that the parties concerned will following the principle of "land for peace', show a flexible and pragmatic attitude and continue their efforts," said foreign ministry spokesman Shen Guofang.
The former colonial powers in the region, France and Britain, said the long-awaited Hebron agreement should pave the way to other pacts to bolster the Middle East peace process.

"This agreement should be a new departure for all aspects of the peace process," said a French foreign ministry statement. "Other parts of the interim accord on the autonomy of the West Bank and Gaza should now be quickly implemented,"
Britain welcomed the agreement to redeploy Israeli troops, saying it was essential in unblocking the peace process.

"It is important to move on swiftly now to other outstanding elements of the interim agreement," said a statement from British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind. "The peace process must continue to move forward."

But Shamir savaged the deal, calling it a defeat for Israel. "This accord is very bad for Israel, it's defeat we have inflicted upon ourselves," Shamir, hardline prime minister from 1986 to 1992, told France's Europe 1 radio.

Aged 81 and former head of Netanyahu's right-wing Likud Party, Shamir predicted the accord would prompt more violence and would collapse. "I don't think that (the accord) will last a long time," he said.

Hebron is home to 400 militant Jewish settlers and 100,000 Palestinians. It was due to be given self-rule 10 months ago but violence and Israel's election of a new right-wing government in June contributed to the delay.
